title: Did Bessent Just Put A Cap On The US Dollar?
text:
Did Bessent Just Put A Cap On The US Dollar?

Louis-Vincent Gave

Gavekal Research | 20 Aug 2026

In the run-up to the last presidential US election, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent liked to highlight what he felt was Janet Yellen’s massive mistake in not extending the duration of outstanding US debt when long-term rates were at record lows. Yesterday, and with the 30-year yield at its highest level in two decades, the US Treasury announced that, starting next month, it would be doubling its buyback operations for long-dated bonds—the 10- to 30-year tenors—from a US$2bn maximum per operation to US$4bn. This sudden announcement came exactly two weeks after the US Treasury had already set the quarter’s buyback plan. If nothing else, this sudden shift in buyback plans indicates that the US Treasury is worried about the breakout in long-dated yields and does not intend to sit back and do nothing. A messaging that triggered some sharp market moves:The above reactions all make sense. After all, a US Treasury actively signaling that it is looking to cap long-term yields is bearish news for the US dollar (there is no free lunch, see The Scott Bessent Scorecard). The more important question is now whether the US Treasury will be successful in this endeavor? To be sure, Scott Bessent can embrace the Janet Yellen playbook of issuing short-term debt and eschewing longer-term issuance. But to a large extent, the US Treasury has already been doing this for years. Out of the almost US$40trn in outstanding US debt, over US$13trn is rolling over/has rolled over in 2026 and, depending on forthcoming issuance (and ever-rising budget deficits), we could be looking at roughly the same amount for 2027… So how much more can the US Treasury really do to keep long-dated yields in check without the help of the Federal Reserve (i.e.: another round of quantitative easing aimed at capping long-term yields?). Still, the signaling from the US Treasury matters because it essentially now leaves investors with two possible scenarios.
